author: Ilse Marek
blurb: A foundry hand walks into a management office to ask where her brother went, and does not leave until somebody tells her. Written, drawn, lettered and inked by one woman over fourteen months, printed on paper so coarse you can feel the grain through the sleeve. Banned in two districts, which sold it in the other eighteen.

chapters.text:
The pour, across the whole page. A ladle the size of a car tipping white metal into a mould, and the white is the white of the paper. Marek never drew light. She drew the absence of ink around it, and the top half of this page is bare newsprint and it still burns your eyes at arm's length.

Silhouetted against it, six figures in leathers, identical at this distance, all doing their jobs.

> Number Four Foundry ran three shifts and had done since before the sky changed. The metal did not care what year it was and neither, in the end, did anybody who worked it.

Ground level. A woman lifting her visor. Face wet, hair flattened, a burn scar down one forearm shaped like a run of solder.

MARTA: Where's Tobin.

A man shrugs, not unkindly, already turning back to the work.

MAN: Office wanted him.
MARTA: Office wanted him when.
MAN: Start of shift.

Close on Marta. Nothing on her face at all.

> It was the end of shift.

---

The walk. Nine panels, and in every one she is the same size in the same place, and only the corridor changes behind her: the shop floor, the wash, the yard, the covered way, the stairs, the carpet, the good carpet, the reception, the door.

Nobody says anything for the length of it.

Then her hand on the office door handle, breaking out of the grid and off the edge of the page. The handle is brass. It is the only clean object she has touched all day.

---

The office. Carpet, a desk, a window with a blind half down, and behind the desk a man who stands up when she comes in. He is polite. He is polite for the entire book.

FOREMAN: Marta. You can't be in here in those.
MARTA: Where's my brother.
FOREMAN: Sit down.
MARTA: Where's my brother.

He sits back down himself, which is worse.

FOREMAN: Tobin's been reassigned.

Just the blind, and the light through it, ruled across the carpet in bars.

MARTA: To where.
FOREMAN: I genuinely don't know. That's not me being careful with you. There's a form, it goes up, it doesn't come back. I sign it and it's gone.

His hands, clean, shaking very slightly. Three short repeated lines at the knuckle, and it is the whole man.

FOREMAN: Sixty this year.
MARTA: Sixty.
FOREMAN: Sixty-one, with him.

She has not moved.

FOREMAN: I have asked. I want you to know I have asked.
MARTA: What did they say.
FOREMAN: They said the foundry's throughput is up.

---

Wide and low, from the foreman's eyeline: Marta standing in his office in her leathers with the light behind her. It is the cover of the issue, exactly, except that on the cover she is holding a length of rebar and here her hands are empty. Nobody notices that until the second reading.

MARTA: Give me the form.
FOREMAN: There isn't a copy.
MARTA: Give me the one you signed.
FOREMAN: Marta.
MARTA: You said you sign it. So you had it in your hand. So you read a name and a number and a place, and you are going to give me the place.

He looks at the blind.

He looks at the blind.

He tells her.

We do not get the word. Marek draws the balloon and leaves it empty. No ellipsis, no scratched-out lettering, just white, and for eighty years people have said this was a printing fault and for eighty years the people who know have said it was not.
chapters.title: Heat

chapters.text:
Night, and a road out of the district drawn from life, so that everyone who has walked it recognises the third telegraph pole.

Marta walking. Still in leathers. Carrying nothing.

> She did not go home first. People have made a great deal of this. She did not go home first because home was two streets the wrong way and she was already walking, and that is all it was.

A gate. Chain-link, three metres, wire along the top, and beyond it a yard of nothing much: sheds, a hardstand, a lit window.

A guard hut, and a man inside with the small blue light of a screen on his face.

MARTA: I'm here for Tobin Vey.
GUARD: There's no.
MARTA: I know there's no. I'm here anyway.

He looks at her properly for the first time. Young, bored, cold, not a monster, wearing a coat that doesn't fit.

GUARD: Go home.
MARTA: What is this place.
GUARD: Go home.
MARTA: You don't know either.

He doesn't answer. He goes back to the screen, and the blue light comes back up on his face.

---

She sits down against the fence.

She is still sitting against the fence. The light in the hut has changed colour, so it is later.

Still sitting. Frost on the wire.

Still sitting. Dawn coming up behind the sheds, drawn with the same bare-paper trick as the pour, so that the sunrise and the molten metal are the same mark on the page.

> She sat at that gate for nine days. Everything you have heard about what she did on the tenth is somebody's uncle's version. Here is what she did.

---

A truck at the gate. Sheeted flatbed, ordinary.

She stands up. Nine days of stiff, and the stiff is drawn: the hand on the fence, the slow unfolding, the second where the knee doesn't take it.

She walks to the middle of the road.

She stands in the middle of the road.

The truck, the gate, the guard hut, the woman in the road, and a lot of empty asphalt.

~HRAAAAAM~

She does not move.

The driver's window comes down. He is fifty, he is tired, he has a flask on the dash.

DRIVER: I don't want this.
MARTA: Neither do I.
DRIVER: I've got a run.
MARTA: I've got a brother.

He looks at the gate. He looks at the guard hut. He looks at the flask.

He turns the engine off.

---

The guard is out of the hut.

The guard is on the phone.

Another truck arrives behind the first, and stops, because the first one has stopped.

Another.

Another.

Then the whole road out of Number Four seen from the height of the water tower, and it is trucks, all the way back to the district, all of them stopped, all of them with their engines off. One woman standing in the middle of the road at the top of the frame, about four millimetres tall.

> Throughput, that week, was not up.
chapters.title: The Gate

chapters.text:
An office. Not the foreman's. A better one, high up, with a window that has a view and a carpet that has never had a boot on it.

Two men and a woman on one side of a table. Marta on the other, still in the leathers, nine days of gate on her.

> They brought her inside, in the end, because a woman standing in a road is a photograph and a woman sitting at a table is a negotiation, and they had people whose whole job was knowing the difference.

EXECUTIVE: We can find your brother.
MARTA: Then find him.
EXECUTIVE: I said we can. I didn't say we would like to, and I didn't say it was free.

She waits.

EXECUTIVE: You go back to your shift. The road clears. The road clears today, and it clears because you cleared it, and people see you clear it. And in a week, quietly, without a photograph, your brother comes home.

Close on Marta, and her shoulder comes down four millimetres.

MARTA: And the other sixty.
EXECUTIVE: I'm sorry?
MARTA: Sixty this year. He said sixty. Sixty-one with mine.

The executive's face does not change, and it goes on not changing across four identical panels, which on cheap paper looks like a printing error and is the cruellest thing in the book.

---

EXECUTIVE: One.
MARTA: Sixty-one.
EXECUTIVE: One. That is the offer. It is a very good offer and it is the only one, and I would like you to understand that I am not being cruel, I am being accurate. I can produce one man. I cannot produce sixty. Nobody in this building can produce sixty. You are asking me for a thing that does not exist and refusing a thing that does.

Silence.

Silence.

Marta stands up.

---

The corridor, nine panels again, in reverse: the good carpet, the carpet, the stairs, the covered way, the yard, the wash, the shop floor. Same size, same place, every panel.

In the eighth she picks up a length of rebar from a stack by the wall without breaking stride. There is no close-up and no change of angle. It is simply in her hand in the eighth panel and it was not in the seventh.

In the ninth, the doorway to the pour, and the white of the paper coming up behind her.

---

The cover image at last, for real, with no panel and no border: Marta in the doorway of the foundry with the light behind her and the rebar held down at her side like a staff.

Under it, small, bottom right, in Marek's own lettering, because Marek lettered everything herself:

> SHE WAS SOMEBODY'S SISTER FIRST. SHE WAS SIXTY-ONE PEOPLE'S SISTER BY FRIDAY.

> CONTINUED

---

> On the inside back cover of the first printing, removed from every edition after it: I worked Number Four for six years and my brother is not coming home and I am not going to pretend at the end of this that he is. If you have bought this you have given me eight credits and I have given you the truth with a woman drawn over the top of it so you would pick it up. I am sorry about that. It was the only way I could think of.

> I. M.
